title: Long story
context: A wavy line of hundreds of tiny bones, from a small head to a thin tip.
question: What is it?

img.author: Josef Maria Eder and Eduard Valenta (1896), The Metropolitan Museum of Art
img.alt: A long curving snake skeleton made of hundreds of small vertebrae.

hints: It's a reptile.
It has no legs at all.
why: An 1896 X-ray of an Aesculapian snake, showing its long chain of vertebrae and ribs.
pearl: Some snakes have more than 300 vertebrae, most with a pair of ribs attached. That's why they can bend in every direction.

title: Big bite
context: A deep-bodied river fish with a jaw full of sharp, tight-fitting teeth.
question: What is it?

img.file: FMIB 52308 Radiograph of Serrasalmo rhombeus (Linnaeus) I U M No11650 208 mm From Crab Falls, British Guiana.jpeg
img.author: Carl H. Eigenmann
img.alt: A deep-bodied fish skeleton with a short toothy jaw.

hints: It lives in South American rivers.
Its reputation is worse than it deserves.
why: An early X-ray of a redeye piranha from British Guiana, showing its deep body and toothy jaws.
pearl: Piranhas replace their teeth in batches: they shed all the teeth on one side of the jaw at once, so they're never left toothless.

title: Pocket money
context: A bunch of glossy, egg-shaped shells with toothy slits underneath.
question: What is it?

img.author: Doruk Salancı
img.alt: A group of oval shells with slit openings, in black and white.

hints: They come from sea snails.
They were once used as money.
why: A print made from an X-ray of a group of cowrie shells.
pearl: Cowrie shells were used as money for centuries in parts of Africa, Asia and the Pacific.

title: Spaghetti
context: An incredibly long, thin fish with a beak that splits into two.
question: What is it?

img.author: Sandra J. Raredon, Smithsonian Institution (NMNH Division of Fishes)
img.alt: A very long thin eel skeleton in loops, with a long split beak.

hints: It's named after a long-beaked bird.
It lives in the deep ocean.
why: An X-ray of a slender snipe eel from the Smithsonian collection.
pearl: The slender snipe eel has more vertebrae than almost any other animal: over 750.

title: Prickly pet
context: A small round mammal X-rayed from above. Its coat is not soft.
question: What is it?

img.file: Csipesz - 12 hetes afrikai fehérhasú törpesün (Atelerix albiventris) röntgen képe - felülnézet.JPG
img.author: Varga Viktor
img.alt: A small round mammal skeleton seen from above.

hints: It rolls into a spiky ball.
This one is an African pygmy pet.
why: An X-ray from above of a healthy 12-week-old African pygmy hedgehog named Clip.
pearl: A hedgehog has thousands of spines. They're hollow hairs made of keratin, the same stuff as your fingernails.

title: Little dragon
context: A small armoured creature with spiky winged fins and a long tail.
question: What is it?

img.author: Sandra J. Raredon, Smithsonian Institution (NMNH Division of Fishes)
img.alt: A small armoured fish with wide spiky fins and a segmented tail.

hints: Despite its name, it's a fish.
Its scientific name mentions a dragon.
why: An X-ray of a little dragonfish, also called a seamoth, from the Smithsonian collection.
pearl: Seamoths are covered in bony armour plates and shuffle along the sea floor on stiff fins.

title: Up, up and away
context: Wings out, long legs dangling, feathers and all. X-rayed in 1896.
question: What is it?

img.author: Walter König (1896)
img.alt: A sepia X-ray of a bird with spread wings and dangling legs.

hints: It has a beak.
It could fly.
why: An 1896 X-ray of a fieldfare, a kind of thrush, X-rayed with its feathers on.
pearl: Many birds have hollow bones braced inside like a bridge, so they are strong but light. This X-ray took 22 minutes to make.

title: Colourful character
context: A crested head, grippy feet and a tail curled like a spring.
question: What is it?

img.author: Josef Maria Eder and Eduard Valenta (1896), The Metropolitan Museum of Art
img.alt: A lizard skeleton with a crested head and a tightly curled tail.

hints: It's a lizard that's famous for one party trick.
Its eyes can look in two directions at once.
why: An 1896 X-ray of a crested chameleon, with its curled tail and grasping feet.
pearl: A chameleon's tongue can shoot out to about twice the length of its body to catch insects.

title: Head start
context: A shark with very widely spaced eyes and an unusual head.
question: What is it?

img.author: Sandra J. Raredon, Smithsonian Institution (NMNH Division of Fishes)
img.alt: A shark skeleton with a very wide T-shaped head.

hints: Its eyes sit at each end of its head.
It's named after a tool.
why: An X-ray of a winghead shark, the hammerhead with the widest head of all.
pearl: The winghead shark's head can be almost half as wide as its body is long.

title: Hidden extras
context: A long, snaky fish curled up, with a fearsome set of jaws.
question: What is it?

img.author: Sandra J. Raredon, Smithsonian Institution (NMNH Division of Fishes)
img.alt: A long coiled eel skeleton with a big toothy jaw.

hints: It hides in reef crevices.
It's a fish, not a snake.
why: An X-ray of a viper moray from the Smithsonian collection.
pearl: Moray eels have a second set of jaws in their throat that shoots forward to grab prey and drag it down.

title: Leafy legend
context: Three bony, twiggy fish with long snouts, compared side by side.
question: What is it?

img.author: Josefin Stiller, Nerida Wilson and Greg Rouse
img.alt: Three long, bony fish skeletons with spiky appendages, stacked.

hints: They are close cousins of seahorses.
One kind looks like floating seaweed.
why: X-rays of the three known seadragon species: the leafy, the weedy and the ruby seadragon (found in 2015).
pearl: The ruby seadragon was only discovered in 2015. Like seahorses, seadragon dads carry the eggs, stuck under their tails.

title: Spiky armour
context: Two tiny armoured fish with big serrated spines sticking out sideways.
question: What is it?

img.author: Sandra J. Raredon, Smithsonian Institution (NMNH Division of Fishes)
img.alt: Two small fish with large serrated spines sticking out sideways.

hints: It's named after a pet with whiskers.
This one is a tiny armoured kind from South America.
why: An X-ray of two Physopyxis lyra, tiny armoured catfish from the Amazon.
pearl: Catfish get their name from their whisker-like barbels, which they use to taste and feel for food.

title: Charged up
context: A small plastic gadget with a spring and wires, X-rayed next to a ruler.
question: What is it?

img.author: Sarah Cartwright
img.alt: A small device with springs and wires on blue film, with a ruler above.

hints: It tells you if something still has power.
You put a small cell in it.
why: An X-ray of a battery tester, showing its spring contacts and circuit.
pearl: A battery tester measures how much electrical push (voltage) a battery has left. A fresh AA gives about 1.5 volts.

title: Fishbowl
context: Three little fish, X-rayed in 1896. Two of them are classic pets.
question: What is it?

img.file: Zwei Goldfische und ein Seefisch (Christiceps argentatus) MET DP262481.jpg
img.author: Josef Maria Eder and Eduard Valenta (1896), The Metropolitan Museum of Art
img.alt: Three small fish skeletons on a dark background.

hints: You might win one at a fair.
They're usually orange.
why: An 1896 X-ray of two goldfish and one sea fish.
pearl: The idea that goldfish have a three-second memory is a myth. Experiments show they can remember things for months.

title: Whiskers
context: A small mammal with a long tail, X-rayed in 1896.
question: What is it?

img.author: Josef Maria Eder and Eduard Valenta (1896), The Metropolitan Museum of Art
img.alt: A small mammal skeleton with a long tail, side on.

hints: It's a rodent.
It's bigger than a mouse.
why: An 1896 X-ray of a rat, from the Vienna X-ray portfolio of Eder and Valenta.
pearl: A rat's front teeth never stop growing. Gnawing keeps them worn down to the right length.

title: Open ocean
context: A big, round, plate-shaped fish from the open ocean.
question: What is it?

img.author: Sandra J. Raredon, Smithsonian Institution (NMNH Division of Fishes)
img.alt: A round, deep-bodied fish skeleton.

hints: It's also called a moonfish.
It's the only fully warm-blooded fish known.
why: An X-ray of an opah, a large round ocean fish.
pearl: In 2015, scientists found the opah is the first known fully warm-blooded fish. It warms its body by flapping its fins.

title: Underwater flier
context: A flat, diamond-shaped body with a thin tail trailing behind.
question: What is it?

img.author: Smithsonian Institution, NMNH Division of Fishes
img.alt: A flat diamond-shaped fish with a long thin tail.

hints: It's a cousin of sharks.
It 'flies' through the water on wing-like fins.
why: An X-ray of a skate from the Smithsonian collection.
pearl: Skates lay eggs in leathery cases called mermaid's purses, which often wash up on beaches.

title: Reef royalty
context: Two tall reef fish X-rayed in 1896. Name the top one.
question: What is it?

img.file: Zanclus cornutus - Acanthurus nigros MET DP262480.jpg
img.author: Josef Maria Eder and Eduard Valenta (1896), The Metropolitan Museum of Art
img.alt: Two tall disc-shaped reef fish skeletons, one above the other.

hints: It has a very long, trailing back fin.
It shares its name with a statue.
why: An 1896 X-ray of a Moorish idol (top) and a surgeonfish (bottom).
pearl: The surgeonfish at the bottom is named for the scalpel-sharp spines near its tail.

title: Excess baggage
context: A scanner image of electronics with some unexpected passengers hidden inside.
question: What is it?

img.author: US Fish and Wildlife Service, Pacific Southwest Region
img.alt: A colourful scanner image of a speaker with lizard shapes in a box inside.

hints: They were found in socks inside a stereo speaker.
Wildlife officers rescued them.
why: A security X-ray showing Philippine monitor lizards hidden in socks inside a stereo speaker, found by US wildlife investigators.
pearl: Customs and wildlife officers use X-ray scanners to find smuggled animals hidden in luggage and parcels.

title: Living fossil
context: A long, armoured fish with a narrow, toothy snout. Its family is older than the dinosaurs' extinction.
question: What is it?

img.author: Sandra J. Raredon, Smithsonian Institution (NMNH Division of Fishes)
img.alt: A long, narrow fish skeleton with a pointed toothy snout.

hints: Its scales are hard and shiny, like enamel tiles.
It can gulp air at the surface.
why: An X-ray of a tropical gar from the Smithsonian collection.
pearl: Gars can breathe air: they gulp it at the surface and use their swim bladder a bit like a lung, so they survive in warm, oxygen-poor water.

title: Squeak
context: A tiny skeleton with a long thin tail, frozen mid-scurry.
question: What is it?

img.author: Nevit Dilmen
img.alt: A small rodent skeleton with a long tail on a dark background.

hints: It's a small rodent.
Cats chase it in cartoons.
why: An X-ray of a house mouse.
pearl: Mice can squeeze through a gap about the width of a pencil, because their skeletons are small and flexible.

title: Toolbox
context: A long flat snout lined with teeth on both edges, attached to a shark-like body.
question: What is it?

img.author: Sandra J. Raredon, Smithsonian Institution (NMNH Division of Fishes)
img.alt: A fish with a long, flat, toothed snout and a curved tail.

hints: It's a kind of ray, not a shark.
Its snout looks like a tool from the shed.
why: An X-ray of a smalltooth sawfish from the Smithsonian collection, showing its toothed 'saw'.
pearl: A sawfish's saw can sense the tiny electric fields of hidden prey. It then slashes sideways to stun and catch it.

title: Glass garden
context: Delicate shapes on long stems, with every layer showing through.
question: What is it?

img.author: Cadop
img.alt: Two trumpet-shaped flowers with long stamens, see-through like glass.

hints: You might put them in a vase.
Bees visit them.
why: A close-up X-ray of two flowers, showing petals and stamens all at once.
pearl: X-rays pass through thin petals more easily than thick stems, so overlapping layers show up as different shades.

title: Real or fake?
context: Strings of beads, X-rayed in 1896 to settle an argument.
question: What is it?

img.file: 1896 x-rays of Physikalischer Verein, real and fake pearls.tif
img.author: Walter König (1896)
img.alt: Several strings of round beads in a sepia X-ray.

hints: Some are real and some are fakes.
Oysters make the real ones.
why: An 1896 X-ray comparing real pearls (middle) with fake ones (left and right).
pearl: Jewellers still use X-rays to tell natural pearls from cultured or fake ones, by looking at the layers inside.

title: Branching out
context: A lacy, fan-shaped net of branches, shadowed on X-ray film.
question: What is it?

img.author: Michel Royon
img.alt: A lacy fan of fine branches on a dark background.

hints: It lives on reefs in the sea.
It's an animal, though it looks like a plant.
why: A shadow picture of a sea fan (gorgonian coral) made on X-ray film.
pearl: A sea fan is a colony of thousands of tiny animals called polyps, sharing one lacy skeleton.

title: Glow in the dark
context: A small, flat-sided deep-sea fish with a deep belly and big upturned eyes.
question: What is it?

img.author: Sandra J. Raredon, Smithsonian Institution (NMNH Division of Fishes)
img.alt: A small, deep-bodied fish skeleton with a sharp belly, shaped like a hatchet.

hints: It makes its own light.
It's named after a tool for chopping wood.
why: An X-ray of a deep-sea hatchetfish from the Smithsonian collection.
pearl: Hatchetfish glow from light organs on their bellies. It matches the faint light from above, so predators below can't see their silhouette.

title: Count on it
context: Rows of tiny chips joined by wires finer than a hair, from the 1970s.
question: What is it?

img.author: G1MFG
img.alt: A row of small chips connected by fine wires to metal pins.

hints: It shows numbers.
Each digit is made from seven little bars.
why: An X-ray of an eight-digit LED display from a 1970s calculator. Fine wires connect each tiny digit.
pearl: A seven-segment display can show any digit from 0 to 9 by lighting different combinations of seven bars.

title: Leggy
context: A round body with jointed legs bending in from the corners.
question: What is it?

img.author: Excillum AB
img.alt: A close-up X-ray of a spider's round body with jointed legs.

hints: It has eight legs.
It spins silk.
why: A high-detail phase-contrast X-ray of a spider's body and legs.
pearl: Spiders have no bones. Their skeleton is on the outside, so they have to shed it to grow.

title: Sun lover
context: Four sprawling legs, a pointed head and a very long tail. X-rayed in 1896.
question: What is it?

img.author: Josef Maria Eder and Eduard Valenta (1896), The Metropolitan Museum of Art
img.alt: A lizard skeleton with four legs and a long tail.

hints: It's a reptile.
It likes basking on warm rocks.
why: An 1896 X-ray of a green lizard from the Eder and Valenta portfolio.
pearl: Many lizards can drop their tail to escape a predator. The tail keeps wriggling as a distraction, and a new one grows back.

title: Odd couple
context: Two museum animals X-rayed together in 1896. Name the one on the left.
question: What is it?

img.file: 1896 x-rays of Physikalischer Verein, turtle and snake.tif
img.author: Walter König (1896)
img.alt: A rounded turtle on the left and a coiled snake on the right.

hints: It carries its house on its back.
Its neighbour in the picture is a coiled snake.
why: An 1896 X-ray of a small turtle (left) and a coiled snake (right) from Frankfurt's Senckenberg Museum.
pearl: A turtle's shell is part of its skeleton: its ribs and backbone are fused to it, so it can never climb out.

title: Razor edge
context: A thin, very deep-bodied fish with a sharp belly edge.
question: What is it?

img.author: Sandra J. Raredon, Smithsonian Institution (NMNH Division of Fishes)
img.alt: A deep, rounded fish skeleton with a sharp keel along the belly.

hints: It's flat like a disc and silver in real life.
It's the only living species in its family.
why: An X-ray of a moonfish (Mene maculata) from the Smithsonian collection.
pearl: The moonfish is the only living member of its fish family. Its relatives are known only from fossils.
